articles.title: Repaying a Bitcoin-backed loan on Sui can leave you waiting to withdraw native BTC
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Fluid’s Sui market lets Bitcoin holders pledge hBTC as collateral and borrow USDC.
- After reclaiming hBTC, a borrower needs Hashi’s validator committee and Guardian to sign the Bitcoin payout.
- Hashi can delay approved requests while capacity refills and skips withdrawals above its configured maximum.
Once a Fluid borrower has repaid their USDC loan and reclaimed eligible hBTC collateral, they hold a Bitcoin-backed token on Sui. To get native Bitcoin into their wallet, they need a separate redemption from Hashi, the protocol that issues hBTC. Hashi’s payout limit can hold up an approved withdrawal even when the pool has enough BTC to cover it.
Fluid announced its hBTC lending markets on Nov. 20, a day after the Sui Foundation announced the market was live. Bitcoin holders can deposit BTC with Hashi, receive hBTC on the Sui network and pledge that token to borrow USDC, the first stablecoin available through the market.
The underlying coins remain on Bitcoin at an address derived for the depositor’s Sui account. Hashi’s deposit guide describes who can spend them in the normal withdrawal process. Validators in Hashi’s committee provide one authorization collectively, and a separate signer called the Guardian provides the other. Once the borrower has the hBTC back on Sui, those signers still have to authorize the Bitcoin payout.
Once a borrower has the hBTC back, they can request a withdrawal on Sui by submitting the amount and a compatible Bitcoin address. Hashi sets the hBTC aside and queues the request while it waits for a quorum of committee members to approve the request. The committee leader gathers approved requests into a batch so several users can receive Bitcoin in a single transaction.
Hashi burns the hBTC when the leader commits the batch. The committee jointly produces one signature for each Bitcoin input the batch spends. The Guardian checks the batch against its limit and supplies a second signature for each input. Once the transaction is fully signed, the leader broadcasts it, with each user’s share of the miner fee deducted from their payout. Hashi marks the withdrawal confirmed after the transaction reaches its required number of Bitcoin confirmations.
What can delay a Bitcoin payout
The Guardian’s withdrawal limit has two settings. One sets the maximum amount the system can release at once. The other determines how quickly capacity refills after a payout batch uses it. The pool balance measures the Bitcoin held by Hashi, while the limit governs how much of that Bitcoin can move at a given time.
If an approved request is within the maximum but is too large for the capacity available at that moment, it waits for room to open up. Requests behind it can wait too. Hashi skips requests above the maximum until governance raises the limit. The borrower can cancel and recover their hBTC after a cooldown, up until the leader commits the request to a batch.
Hashi describes roughly five minutes from submission as one trigger for building a batch. The full withdrawal also depends on approval, available payout capacity, signatures and Bitcoin confirmations. Hashi’s withdrawal FAQ describes how to check current capacity. The deployed maximum and refill rate remain unverified, as does the time from repayment to a Bitcoin payout for a Fluid borrower.
On Nov. 21, Merkl’s Fluid lending campaign displayed $862.26K in total value locked in its Sui fUSDC rewards opportunity. The figure captures activity on the lender side of the market. The amount of USDC borrowers have drawn against hBTC remains unverified.
Fluid says Anchorage Digital’s institutional clients can lend USDC or borrow it against hBTC on the protocol. Anchorage Digital Bank N.A. provides custody and settlement services. The Sui Foundation says institutions can already use Anchorage’s self-custody wallet, Porto, to access hBTC and select Fluid strategies. It expects tri-party settlement in early 2027. Anchorage identifies Atlas as its tri-party route for institutions that keep assets in qualified custody.

articles.title: Claude-assisted proof of Riemann hypothesis validated by independent checkers
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The Lean and Mathlib communities said independent checks validated Levent Alpöge’s Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
- A clean rebuild reproduced the proof export byte for byte, and separate tools matched the theorem and checked the proof steps.
- Clay still listed the conjecture as unsolved on Nov. 22, and prize consideration requires qualifying publication and broad acceptance.
Independent checkers validated Levent Alpöge’s Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the Lean and Mathlib communities said on Nov. 21. Teams rebuilt his roughly 17-million-line library, matched its conclusion to the original conjecture and checked each step of the exported proof. They established what the code proved while a complete mathematical write-up was still to come.
The conjecture dates to 1859. It says that when the Riemann zeta function equals zero, the solutions other than a known set of exceptions all lie on the same vertical line, where the real part is one-half. Where those zeros lie helps explain how the distribution of prime numbers deviates from its average pattern.
Alpöge released the proof on Nov. 20 as code for Lean, a system for writing and checking mathematical proofs. In his release note, he said he chose a setting where two mathematical ideas could be combined and credited Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude with suggesting advances late in the argument.
How the teams checked the proof
In his MIT-hosted verification logs, Andrew Sutherland reported that a rebuild on a separate machine, with networking disabled and the source files set to read-only, produced a byte-for-byte match to the published proof export. The export contains the formal proof steps in a form that other checkers can read.
In their joint statement, the Lean and Mathlib communities said they put the target theorem in a separate challenge file that imported only Mathlib, Lean’s library of formalized mathematics. Two comparison tools confirmed that the conclusion in Alpöge’s proof matched Mathlib’s existing statement of the conjecture.
Two independently written checkers, nanoda and con-leche, accepted the full export, Sutherland reported. They checked whether the steps justified the conclusion using the exported data, which kept executable code in the original source files out of that part of the process.
Sutherland’s team also replayed all 175,187 compiled modules through Lean’s own checker. The team’s additional Lean runs on the raw export were still underway in his Nov. 22 update. The checks also covered a generalized version of the conjecture for Dirichlet L-functions.
Alpöge said he planned to write up the proof for mathematicians to read. Michael Rubinstein at the University of Waterloo posted a working guide dated Nov. 21 that explains parts of the argument for the original conjecture. The guide still relies on the Lean development for the proof of a central inequality.
Clay Mathematics Institute’s problem page still listed the conjecture as unsolved when checked on Nov. 22. Under Clay’s prize rules, the institute considers a proposed solution only after publication in a qualifying outlet, at least two years since that publication and general acceptance in the global mathematics community.

articles.title: AI banking agent scored 100% on its own tests then failed 92 of 97 real-world simulations
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Uniphore researchers found that 86 of 132 builds with recorded self-tests scored at least 99% on tests their builders wrote.
- In 13 Claude Opus 4.8 builds with revisions, gains averaged 16.9 percentage points on their own tests and 3.2 on withheld cases.
- Switching the test-and-revise loop on or off showed no statistically significant effect on withheld scores in a 252-build comparison.
AI systems tasked with building business agents often gave their work near-perfect grades on tests they wrote themselves. In a Nov. 19 preprint, researchers at Uniphore found that the grades could improve far more than scores on cases withheld from the builders during development.
The researchers used AppSci-Bench, a benchmark that puts AI builders to work in seven simulated business workflows, including invoice review, customer relationship management and airline rebooking. A builder could ask a simulated business user what the agent needed to do, then develop it using the tools and data available in that setting.
In the test runs that allowed revisions, builders could write their own tests and keep changes that raised the score. After the builder submitted an agent, the benchmark ran it on separate cases withheld during development. The researchers released the benchmark code and recorded results alongside the preprint.
What the builders’ tests missed
Uniphore researchers found that 86 of the 132 builds with a recorded self-test scored at least 99% on the tests their builders wrote. The researchers tracked 13 Claude Opus 4.8 builds that could revise their agents, comparing the first round of testing with the last. For those builds, scores rose an average of 16.9 points on tests the model wrote and 3.2 points on the withheld cases. In six of the 24 revision steps the researchers examined in that subset, the builder's grade rose while the withheld-case score held steady.
In a broader comparison of 252 builds using Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in withheld-case scores when they switched the test-and-revise loop on or off. That result held in both the researchers’ setup and the models’ native coding tools, Claude Code and Codex, after accounting for multiple comparisons.
One banking build showed how a test could reinforce a bad assumption. GPT-5.5 assumed it could not look customers up by email or name even though both options were available. One test it wrote rewarded asking for a customer ID, and the agent ended up refusing the other lookups. The agent eventually scored a perfect 1.0 on its builder’s tests. In the withheld trial the researchers examined, it succeeded on five of 97 cases.
Meta used a live search test after its AI agents screened candidate changes offline.
For a team evaluating a banking agent, a test that supplies only an email address could expose the same blind spot. Keeping a set of cases outside development lets the team see how the submitted agent handles situations its builder’s tests may never have covered.

articles.title: Bithumb halts CYBER deposits and withdrawals while trading stays open
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Bithumb suspended CYBER deposits and withdrawals after flagging a suspected security issue and said trading would remain available.
- Bithumb said it would credit deposits received during the pause in sequence after service resumed.
- Kraken warned that CYBER deposits via Optimism could be delayed and said other funding methods were operating normally.
Bithumb suspended deposits and withdrawals of the CYBER token after flagging signs of a possible security issue. The exchange said customers could still trade CYBER already held in their accounts. Kraken separately warned of possible delays for CYBER deposits sent over the Optimism network.
Bithumb set the cutoff for 2:18 a.m. Korea time on Nov. 22, or 17:18 UTC on Nov. 21. Seven minutes after the scheduled cutoff, the exchange confirmed that the pause was in effect. It also urged customers to take care when trading CYBER, saying the security concern could lead to sharper price swings.
For users who had already sent CYBER to Bithumb, the cutoff mattered because sending a deposit and seeing it credited to an account can happen at different times. Bithumb said network congestion or slow confirmations could hold up credit even for transfers sent before the cutoff. It said it would credit deposits received during the suspension in sequence once service resumed.
Customers who had requested a withdrawal before the cutoff and were still waiting for it to complete faced a separate process. Bithumb said it would run system checks and process those requests in sequence, which could delay the account update. The exchange’s processing note applied to requests already in its system when the suspension took effect. New CYBER withdrawals remained subject to the pause.
Bithumb said it would reopen transfers once the network was stable and would post the reopening in the same notice. It gave no reopening time.
Kraken warns of Optimism deposit delays
Kraken flagged possible CYBER deposit delays on Optimism at 19:59 UTC on Nov. 21 and said its other funding methods were operating normally.
The incident page still listed the issue as identified at 18:12 UTC on Nov. 22, with no resolution posted. Kraken’s update left the cause and timing of a fix open.

articles.title: Senators want state-licensed firms to keep issuing stablecoins after Jan. 18
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Six senators asked Treasury to protect state-regulated stablecoin issuers as the GENIUS Act begins to restrict U.S. issuance in January.
- Eligible federal applicants could keep issuing only if a federal regulator grants a waiver that covers the issuance restriction.
- New York says qualifying issuers can keep issuing during state review. The general restriction on U.S. platform sales starts in July 2028.
Six senators are asking Treasury to let qualifying state-regulated stablecoin issuers keep putting new tokens into circulation while their states’ rules are under federal review. The GENIUS Act takes effect on January 18, 2027. Treasury’s proposal recognizes temporary relief for eligible federal applicants that get a waiver. It leaves open what happens if a state’s regulatory framework still awaits certification.
Sens. Cynthia Lummis and Kirsten Gillibrand led the bipartisan November 17 letter, which Lummis’s office released November 18. They asked Treasury for temporary protection during certification for issuers in states that will have a qualifying framework in place before January 18, 2028. They warned that a clearer federal route could steer issuers toward a federal license.
The proposed Section 3 rule would recognize relief for two groups with applications pending when the law takes effect. One is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution whose parent has applied on its behalf. The other is an applicant seeking to become a federally qualified payment stablecoin issuer. The primary federal regulator must grant a waiver, and its terms must cover the relevant Section 3 restriction. Relief can run for up to 12 months from the law’s effective date.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has a separate final rule that requires a written request and a substantially complete issuer application pending on or before January 18, 2027. It can grant relief on public-interest grounds or in extraordinary circumstances. Its licensing page says it has yet to open applications or waiver requests and is awaiting clearance for its application forms.
Treasury’s proposal treats the first transfer that gives someone outside the issuer the right to use, transfer or redeem the token as issuance. An issuer could create tokens for its own inventory and still face a restriction when it tries to put those tokens into circulation.
The OCC waiver rule gives active issuers a route to request temporary relief before the January deadline.
New York and the senators differ on what state issuers need
Treasury asked whether issuers should get relief before a state files for certification or while a review is pending. Four state regulatory and legislative groups asked for such protection in October. New York’s Department of Financial Services offered a different reading. It says qualifying issuers can keep issuing if their state’s rules are substantially similar and the state files within a year, until any final denial. It wants Treasury to confirm that reading in the final rule.
In the preamble to its interim rule, the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee described the state option for issuers with $10 billion or less in consolidated outstanding stablecoin issuance as requiring a state filing and committee approval. The committee has 30 days to decide once a complete certification has been submitted. It will seek to expedite initial reviews after the Act takes effect for states that had a qualifying regime in place by January 14, 2026. New York says it expects to qualify for expedited review. The initial state filing is due within a year of the Act taking effect.
The committee says it will start accepting certifications once the forms clear federal review. The paperwork record still shows the certification forms under review. If Treasury treats committee approval as a prerequisite and offers no temporary relief, issuers that depend on the state route could have to wait to issue new units.
New York’s approvals show why the legal issuer matters. The state’s Greenlist and charter register identify Ripple USD (RLUSD) and WisdomTree Dollar (USDW) as approved for issuance in the state. Ripple’s November 16 terms name Ripple Custody & Trust Co., the trade name of New York-chartered Standard Custody & Trust Company, LLC, as the RLUSD issuer.
The OCC charter record shows that Ripple National Trust Bank’s charter became effective October 26. Ripple said Standard Custody would continue issuing RLUSD, with the separate national bank authorized to manage reserves and provide custody.
WisdomTree identifies a different New York trust, WisdomTree Digital Trust Company, LLC, as USDW’s issuer. For either coin, a federal waiver would have to cover issuance by the legal issuer.
ZUSD still appears on the Greenlist. Its issuer, GMO-Z.com Trust Company, Inc., removed the mint function in May during a voluntary wind-down. The issuer said direct redemptions ended November 11 and that remaining balances are subject to mandatory redemption. ZUSD’s wind-down was already underway months before Treasury published its proposal.
Exchanges face a separate July 2028 deadline
Under the GENIUS Act, January 18, 2027 is the effective date for the U.S. issuance restriction. If a state-regulated issuer has to pause, the immediate effect would be on its ability to supply fresh units to customers and distributors. Trading already-issued tokens and redeeming them with the issuer are separate activities.
Starting July 18, 2028, digital asset service providers such as exchanges generally can offer or sell payment stablecoins to people in the U.S. only if the issuer is permitted or an exception applies.
A separate foreign-issuer provision applies from the Act’s effective date. It conditions U.S. platform availability on the foreign issuer’s ability and commitment to comply with lawful orders and reciprocal arrangements. Section 18 also provides a route for foreign issuers from comparable regimes that register with the OCC and meet other conditions.

articles.title: Trump Dinner Wallets Linked to Non-US Crypto Exchanges
articles.text:
Half of wallets on Trump’s dinner list got tokens from non-US exchanges
Public Citizen traced 66 of 130 qualifying wallets to exchanges that restrict US users, raising questions over who is attending Trump’s memecoin dinner on Sunday.
More than half the wallets that qualified for Donald Trump’s memecoin dinner on Sunday received TRUMP tokens from crypto exchanges that bar US users, according to analysis from consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
Trump is hosting his second dinner for his top memecoin holders at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, more than a year after an inaugural dinner in May 2025. The dinner offers up to 185 seats based on time-weighted TRUMP holdings.
Public Citizen said it traced 66 of the 130 wallets on the public leaderboard to exchanges including Binance (the global exchange), Bybit and BloFin — which are not permitted to serve US citizens. The list also included 15 of the 29 wallets that qualified for a VIP reception with the president.
“If those bans are enforced, many of the people vying for a seat at the president’s table don’t live in the United States,” said Public Citizen research director Zach Everson.
Trump’s memecoin events have drawn scrutiny over whether foreign buyers can essentially buy access to the president. Democratic lawmakers called on the White House to release the guest list for the first dinner in May 2025, while some joined a protest outside the golf club. They renewed the request again in October.
Who qualified for Trump’s memecoin dinner?
FastX, a Singapore-linked crypto trading platform, was the top-ranked wallet, holding $1.65 million in TRUMP at the time of the snapshot on Nov. 16.
The third highest ranked wallet has been linked to Unitas, a stablecoin issuer run by a British Virgin Islands company, according to Public Citizen.
Morten Christensen, a crypto entrepreneur from the Netherlands and founder and CEO of AirdropAlert, shared a picture from the Trump gala dinner on X. He came 26th with $45,351 in time-weighted TRUMP holdings.
Public Citizen also identified 14 wallets it suspects were controlled by the same person or group. Each received approximately 3,700 TRUMP tokens from Binance in October before being emptied weeks ahead of the cutoff.
Related: ‘Lawyer up’: Democrats target Trump, Big Tech after midterm sweep
Tron founder Justin Sun, the top-ranked holder at the May 2025 dinner, was expected to skip the event, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Meanwhile, Trump is a featured speaker for the event, and guests also include Floyd Mayweather, “Shark Tank” investor Kevin O’Leary, former NBA player Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard.
Trump token down 99% from peak
The gala dinner comes even as the TRUMP token trades 98.8% below its all-time high of $75.35.
Trump held the first dinner for TRUMP holders in May 2025 at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, when the token was trading at $14.43. By the time he held his second memecoin event, a conference and luncheon at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, the token had already dropped to $2.88.
As of the time of writing, the TRUMP token is trading at $0.89.

articles.title: XRP Ledger trial settled 213,000 paid AI requests in 6,324 transactions
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Two checks cashed on November 18 paid the same AI service in RLUSD, and t54 Labs identified both as batches.
- t54 Labs reported an average fee of 0.36 drops per paid request in its October beta, against a 10-drop benchmark.
- Repeat check cashing across more merchants and the amount of RLUSD they receive would show whether the beta is gaining broader use.
Two checks cashed on the XRP Ledger on Nov. 18 paid the same AI service in RLUSD. Payments company t54 Labs identified both as batches. In its closed October beta, t54 reported that bundling requests cut the average network fee to 0.36 drops of XRP per paid call.
The checks delivered 0.31 RLUSD and 0.46 RLUSD to the same ledger address. The XRPL AI Hub, run by t54 Labs, identifies the merchant as Heurist Inference Router and classifies both transfers as batches.
The first check and second check came from different payer addresses. Each had a spending ceiling of 1 RLUSD. The ledger charged 12 drops of XRP to open each check and 12 to cash it, for a total of 24 drops per pair.
A drop is one millionth of an XRP. The Hub marks payment intent as unverified in its first receipt and its second receipt. The receipts give no call counts, so the November fee per request remains unknown.
t54 Labs reported that its mainnet beta settled 213,008 paid requests across 3,162 sessions using 6,324 ledger transactions from Oct. 14 to 17. It put the average network fee at about 0.36 drops per paid request. Its benchmark was a single transaction per request at the ledger's standard minimum fee of 10 drops, which can rise under load.
In t54's beta, the payer first opens a check on the ledger with a maximum amount. A session key authorizes each charge off-ledger as the agent makes paid requests. At the end of the session, the merchant cashes the check once for the amount used. Each completed session takes two ledger transactions, so adding requests to a session spreads those two fees over more charges.
The beta began on mainnet in October with RLUSD as its only settlement asset. t54 says it is limited to onboarded merchants and registered payers, and its developer guide still describes sessions as part of internal merchant testing. The public facilitator has yet to offer batch sessions, according to t54.
What XRP Ledger payers need to hold
An open check adds 0.2 XRP to the payer's reserve requirement on top of the regular 1 XRP account reserve. That amount remains in the account while the check is open. A payer with several checks open at once needs the extra reserve for each one. The reserve requirement falls when the check is cashed or canceled. Expiration alone leaves the check on the ledger until someone cancels it.
The ledger records show that pattern in both November examples. Each payer's count of owned ledger objects rose by one when the check opened and returned to its earlier level after cashing.
The RLUSD principal moves at cashing. The ceiling caps what the merchant can collect, and the payer needs enough funds when the merchant submits the check.
On Nov. 22, XRP traded at about $0.93, according to CryptoSlate’s XRP price data.
To see whether use is spreading beyond Heurist, watch how many distinct merchants cash checks repeatedly and how much RLUSD they receive. The XRPL AI Hub dashboard reports settlement value in dollars and lists registered merchants separately. t54 counts each batch as one settlement, so settlement counts can grow more slowly than paid requests.
The xrpl.fi x402 tracker counts standard Payment transactions carrying t54’s tag and memo, a filter that excludes the two Heurist checks. The earlier XRPL AI Hub figures illustrate how request counts and settlement activity can tell different stories. Gauging whether merchants are handling more requests per check requires off-ledger request counts.

articles.title: Will Bitcoin’s Big Rebound Hold? More Tampered Ledgers Found: Hodler’s Digest
articles.text:
Will Bitcoin’s big rebound hold? More tampered Ledgers found: Hodler’s Digest
Bitcoin rebounds sharply from its new cycle low, but is $55,111 really the bottom? Ledger investigates new reports of tampered devices in Berlin and the UAE.
Bitcoin’s 11% rebound, Kraken says everything’s fine despite $17K Bitcoin price
Bitcoin saw a sharp recovery on the weekend to $61,034, marking an 11% rebound from its new cycle low around $55,111 on Coinbase. But will it hold?
It wasn’t a crypto only crash however, as concerns grow over the sustainability of the debt-financed AI build out. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell another 5.3% on Friday and is on the verge of a bear market, having dropped almost 20% from its October peak. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% last week, for the 12th worst week since 1952, and gold lost another 4.3% in the past 24 hours, to be 21.6% down since September.
At the time of writing Bitcoin’s price was holding steady around $60,750 but there are plenty of predictions it has further to fall. Many point to historical parallels with previous four year cycles, which bottomed after the US mid-terms.
Earlier in the week veteran trader Peter Brandt noted that:
“Every bull market phase in BTC’s history has ended with at least a 75% correction of the previous parabolic bull trend. Could this be what’s happening in Bitcoin?”
The future arrived early on Kraken’s Canadian dollar markets when the BTC price briefly crashed to around US$17,000. Despite the price being 71% below its USD market, Kraken said everything was fine, every order was processed correctly and its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts. “Executed trades stand,” Kraken said.
Crypto influencer Cryptobull offered a tiny bit of hopium when he pointed out that Bitcoin’s Market Value to Realized Valu (MVRV) peak this cycle only reached 2.29 times above its cost basis, and if you extrapolate that to the cycle low, it would come in at around 1.03 times the cost basis of $53,700. Which would be almost exactly the $55,130 price that Bitcoin just hit.
Unfortunately, cycle theorist Benjamin Cowen says that in bear markets Bitcoin usually ends up much lower than the realized price — and drops down to the balanced price, which Coinglass puts at $38.7K.
Source: Coinbase
Tampered Ledgers reported in Dubai and Germany
Ledger has warned customers who purchased hardware wallets in Berlin since January 2026 to contact its support team as the company investigates reports of tampered devices in Germany and the United Arab Emirates.
Several suspicious devices have been reported in Berlin, while two customers in Dubai reported losing a combined $604,000 in cryptocurrency.
Ledger said the incidents were connected to the same distribution-channel tampering campaign first investigated in Southeast Asia in October. Ledger is also offering physical inspections, including X-ray analysis, at its factory in Vierzon, France, for customers concerned their devices may have been compromised.
Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade could slip to May 2027 over compatibility concerns
Last week Ethlabs was pushing to make Ethereum post quantum and AI proof in 2027. This week’s All Core Devs Call suggested the chain may not even see Glamsterdam activated until May 2027.
Under the current specifications, mainnet activation could come as early as mid-January 2027. However, if modifications to the gas pricing Ethereum Improvement Proposals (EIPs) are adopted and then tested to see if they break contracts, activation could be pushed until late February or early March, or even April or May. No decision has been reached yet.
The call also discussed the possibility of modifying the EIPs in the Hegota fork to prioritize post quantum features, although several devs argued that reducing the upgrade’s scope would offer little benefit unless it also shortened the rollout timeline.
Binance hacker moves nearly $600M in ETH, routes funds through THORChain, Chainflip
Wallets linked to the Binance hack moved nearly $600 million in Ether over two days, with some of the stolen funds routed through cross-chain swap protocols, according to blockchain analysts.
The attackers moved about $248 million ETH to new wallets on Thursday and another $346 million ETH, on Friday. Attackers routed part of the funds through cross-chain protocols THORChain and Chainflip, according to blockchain data provider Onchain Lens.
THORChain’s 24-hour swap volume soared to $239 million on Friday, pushing the protocol’s earnings to $243,000, according to THORChain’s dashboard.
Anthropic shares attract half the net purchases on day one as SpaceX
Retail investors traded $772 million in Anthropic shares on its Nasdaq debut Thursday, but their net purchases totaled just $60 million, about half the $118 million they put into SpaceX on its first day of trading in June.
Anthropic’s first-day retail trading volume topped SpaceX’s $669 million and was the highest for any market debut in Vanda Research’s data, which go back to 2012, Yahoo Finance reported.
Volume counts both purchases and sales, while net buying measures how much purchases exceeded sales.
ANT closed its first day of trading up 17% on the IPO price, but the stock fell to just 7% above the IPO price on day two amid a broad market sell off.
Winners and Losers
At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 6.5% to trade at $60,815, Ethereum (ETH) is down 5.9% to trade at $1,713 and XRP (XRP) is down 4.3% to $0.02. The total market cap is at $2.08 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.
Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Pieverse (PIEVERSE) with a 91.2% gain, Venice Token (VVV) on 28.74%, and Falcon Finance (FF) on 4.1%.
The top three altcoin losers of the week are Sky (SKY) which was down 22.6%, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance (FET) down 18.4% and Aptos (APT) down 16.8%.
Top Prediction of the Week
Bitcoin carry trades could beat Treasury bills in 2027, Sygnum predicts
Bitcoin carry trades could regain their edge over US Treasury bills in 2027 as demand for leverage recovers, according to digital asset bank Sygnum.
In its 2027 outlook, it forecasts that the annualized premium on three-month Bitcoin futures at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange would average more than 2% above three-month US Treasury bill yields next year.
Fabian Dori, chief investment officer at Sygnum, told Cointelegraph that returns could recover as investors become more willing to take risks and fewer hedge funds compete for the same profits.
Top FUD of the Week
Senator Ruben Gallego says the crypto industry put too much money into Republican election campaigns.
IOSCO warns quantum upgrades could slow blockchains, leave security gaps
The International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) warned that upgrading blockchains to withstand quantum attacks could slow transactions and raise fees.
In a report released Thursday, IOSCO said some quantum-resistant digital signatures take up far more space than those used to authorize transactions today. Larger signatures mean fewer transactions can fit in each block, which could increase congestion, push up fees and require more storage.
IOSCO cited an experiment in which a test version of Solana ran about 90% slower with quantum-resistant signatures.
US Senate advances prediction market restrictions with DEATH BETS Act
The US Senate passed legislation Thursday that would prohibit federally regulated prediction markets from offering contracts tied to war, terrorism, assassination and events primarily determined by a person’s death, sending the bill to the House for consideration.
The DEATH BETS Act, introduced by Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff in March, passed by voice vote on Thursday after lawmakers adopted an amendment by unanimous consent.
Sky Protocol sees $2 billion in stablecoin withdrawals, disputes illicit fund claims
Sky Protocol processed more than $2 billion in stablecoin redemptions on Thursday, the same day a CoinDesk investigation linked $518 million in transactions through the protocol to illicit activity.
The withdrawals came amid concerns raised by the investigation that Circle could freeze USDC held by Sky. Sky said on Friday in a statement that USDS maintained its $1 peg throughout the withdrawals and challenged the investigation, pointing to a review by Block Analitica.
Top Magazine Features of the Week
Bitcoin to $1M by 2030? ‘Almost certainly not,’ says Dragonfly’s Qureshi
Dragonfly’s Haseeb Qureshi says Bitcoin could reach $400,000 by 2030 but doubts it will return to $100,000 by year-end with the rout in AI stocks weighing on crypto.
Ethereum’s new DeFi security tool raises questions over censorship
Phylax’s system lets decentralized protocols block potentially harmful transactions, but raises questions about potential censorship and Ethereum’s concentrated builder market.
How to preserve wealth and access funds during a national emergency
As geopolitical and technological threats multiply, the big question is whether you can hold on to your wealth and access funds when the system fails.

articles.title: Onchain FX Could Grow From Small, Real-World Demand
articles.text:
The future of onchain FX could start with users, not institutional liquidity
Onchain FX does not need to recreate the trillion-dollar institutional market to become useful. Real demand can make smaller markets work first.
Opinion by Michael Egorov, founder of Curve Finance and Yield Basis
For a long time, the obvious way to think about onchain foreign exchange (FX) was to start at the top. Banks tokenize currencies, large financial institutions move their FX activity onchain and institutional liquidity naturally follows.
The end result? Blockchain-based FX eventually grows large enough to resemble its traditional counterpart. But that’s not necessarily how it is going to happen.
In fact, there are growing signs that onchain FX will develop in the exact opposite way — from the bottom up.
Stablecoins like Brazilian Digital (BRZ) or Monerium’s EURe can be quickly redeemed onchain and easily moved from digital wallets to bank accounts. They generate healthy trading activity as decentralized finance (DeFi) users swap them in decentralized exchange (DEX) pools.
Markets like this end up developing in real time around a practical user need, which is moving directly between digital currencies and fiat.
This is still just an early-stage example, but the use case and demand are real enough. Keyrock data shows that the majority of onchain stablecoin trades tied to emerging market currencies fall in the $1,000 to $10,000 range — modest amounts compared to institutional scale — but that’s precisely the point.
It shows how the market is building in the general direction of onchain FX to meet practical payment needs, not just large traders.
‘Small’ is not the same as ‘useless’
People and businesses need to move their money between currencies, and clearly, they are not content to wait for major traditional finance (TradFi) institutions to move their FX operations onto blockchain rails.
Related: Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts
There’s a pretty common assumption about onchain FX in that a market needs huge liquidity before it can become really useful. In practice, though, that’s not entirely true.
If there is genuine demand from someone who needs to exchange dollars into euros, Swiss francs or another currency, even a smaller pool can process those transactions and serve a real economic purpose.
Stablecoin DEX Trade Volume. Source: Keyrock Research
Onchain FX doesn’t need to become big before it becomes useful; instead, it can grow precisely because people are actually using it.
As a matter of fact, this is more or less what happened with stablecoins. They began as a relatively niche crypto-native use case, and yet today we already know them to be part of a much broader financial infrastructure.
Chainalysis recently shared data that shows cross-border stablecoin activity jumped to over $220 billion by mid-2026. That’s an almost 80% growth over the course of one year, proving that demand and activity are constantly on the rise. There is no reason onchain FX can’t follow a similar path.
The user does not care how big the market is
This is actually the most practical side of this issue. Onchain FX obviously won’t be able to compete with the entire global foreign exchange market anytime soon; that’s still years away. But the more interesting question is what problems it can solve for someone who already has money onchain.
Today, you can exchange a USD stablecoin into a EUR stablecoin (or some other alternative) onchain and use that money for payments with relatively little trouble. In fact, doing it this way is often faster and cheaper than going with a classic international bank transfer.
Related: Circle’s ARC token sale lifts earnings as lower yields weigh on USDC income
The same logic applies to onchain FX. A fintech or crypto-card company does not need to recreate the entire institutional market; what they need is to move their customers’ funds efficiently between currencies.
When someone is trying to pay in a different currency, converting it can add costs to the operation, since it usually involves Visa or Mastercard, which charge around 1% in processing fees.
Onchain exchanges are a much better option here. If user funds are already living on blockchain rails, swapping USD stablecoins into EUR stablecoins can be done directly, without going through any extra intermediaries, which is both faster and less costly.
Banks will most likely remain important entry and exit points where digital money needs to interact with the real world. Issuing and redeeming local currencies, accessing bank accounts, dealing with compliance and such is where banks will take the lead.
But when the money is actually onchain, many of the traditional “in-between” steps can be dropped for greater efficiency.
From the perspective of a user who just wants to conduct a financial transfer with minimal complications, that’s a highly positive improvement. How big or small the overall market matters little in this case.
Demand is only half the problem
There is, of course, a catch.
Real demand is crucial, but it does not magically solve the problem of liquidity. The challenge is not simply to create a EUR/USD or CHF/USD pool; it’s to make them economically sustainable.
This is where automated market makers can make a difference. Traditional market-making firms may not find it attractive to provide liquidity for a small FX market; there may simply not be enough volume to justify the operational costs.
Cross-border stablecoin flows. Source: Chainalysys
Automated liquidity changes that equation because software can provide liquidity continuously without requiring a market-making firm to manually manage every trade.
Imagine two dollar stablecoins, USDC (USDC) and Tether (USDT). From the perspective of a traditional exchange, moving from one dollar stablecoin into another might look like a fairly boring business. Both assets are supposed to be worth roughly $1, so there isn’t much price movement to trade around.
But if there is still a real need for people to switch between stablecoins like that, an automated market maker can create a pool where users can make that swap directly. Each trade generates a small fee for the liquidity providers, and when enough people need the same conversion, a market can exist even when it doesn’t look particularly exciting to a traditional market maker.
This kind of adoption cannot exactly be called explosive, true, but there’s also nothing wrong with slow, natural growth. Sometimes, new markets just need a small group of people who have a problem the existing infrastructure does not solve particularly well. If those users can make the market economically viable, liquidity can grow from there.
About the author: Michael Egorov is the founder of Curve Finance and Yield Basis. He is also a physicist, entrepreneur and crypto maximalist. Michael transitioned from the scientific field to the crypto industry and holds a bronze medal from the International Physics Olympiad and a PhD in ultracold atoms.

articles.title: AI just exposed a major weakness in anonymous peer reviews
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Claude Fable 5.2 correctly named the writer on 56% of 398 private reviews and meta-reviews supplied by six volunteers.
- In a separate set of 1,559 public reviews, Claude was right on 21.4% of the 1,530 reports it answered.
- The six-person sample shows that an unsigned report can reveal its writer, while leaving the broader risk uncertain.
Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 correctly named the writer of 56% of 398 reviews and meta-reviews in a small test of unsigned peer reviews. Six volunteers wrote the reports. The model saw one report at a time, without web access, tools, a list of possible authors or other writing samples.
In a Nov. 19 preprint, Atrey Desai and colleagues analyzed reports written between 2015 and 2026 for 26 double-blind conferences and workshops in machine learning and natural language processing. The researchers knew who wrote each report, but the reviewers’ names had never been publicly linked to them. In 19 cases, the text itself was already publicly available without a name.
Claude named the writer on 68.4% of 266 standard reviews and 31.1% of 132 meta-reviews, which summarize the reviews of a submission. The meta-reviews were shorter and came from just two of the six contributors. The study did not separate the effects of report length, type and authorship.
The 56% result counts each report equally, so contributors who supplied more reports had more influence on the overall figure. When the researchers gave each reviewer equal weight, Claude’s average accuracy was 49.1%. The test showed that an unsigned report can give its writer away. Estimating how often that happens across confidential peer review would take a larger, more varied sample.
Public reviews yielded a lower overall score
The researchers also tested 1,559 public reviews from 47 open-review journals. Claude correctly identified the reviewer in 21.4% of the 1,530 cases it answered. The paper reports 39.3% accuracy for a subset containing 789 reviews that Pangram 4.1, an AI-text detector, had labeled human or mixed. The paper’s abstract cites that filtered rate, rounded to 39%.
Accuracy was higher on public reviews whose writers cited their own work. Claude recorded 80.2% accuracy in the group of 106 reviews with self-citations and 17.1% in the group of 1,453 without them.
Claude made mistakes even in the group where it performed best. An editor or author presented with a name from Claude would still need independent evidence to establish who wrote an unsigned review. CryptoSlate has also reported on how frontier AI models handled fabricated research data. The team says it plans to add results from a substantially larger set of anonymous peer reviews in an update to the preprint.

articles.title: Today in Crypto: BTC Drops on Kraken, Hong Kong Licensing, Bitcoin Falls Below $60K
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, Bitcoin briefly fell to the equivalent of $17K on Kraken’s Canadian-dollar market, but the exchange ruled out a breach and said all executed trades would stand. Hong Kong has published a bill to expand crypto licensing requirements to custody, advisory, dealing and management services under the SFC’s oversight, while Bitcoin fell below $60,000 for the first time since July amid a broader selloff in US stocks.
Bitcoin briefly drops to $17K on Kraken, exchange upholds trades
Crypto exchange Kraken said it would honor trades executed during a sharp selloff across its Canadian-dollar markets that briefly pushed Bitcoin to the equivalent of about $17,000 on Saturday.
In a statement, Kraken said its Canadian-dollar trading pairs experienced heavy selling pressure starting around 20:00 UTC on Friday, causing prices to fall significantly below those on other markets.
The exchange said every order was processed correctly and its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts. “Executed trades stand,” Kraken said.
Kraken’s BTC/CAD pair fell to $24,250 Canadian during the 15-minute interval beginning at 08:00 UTC on Saturday, according to exchange trading data.
On Friday, the Bank of Canada’s reference rate showed C$1.4325 per US dollar, putting Bitcoin’s low on Kraken’s Canadian-dollar market at about $16,900. This was about 71% below Bitcoin’s price of around $57,650 on Kraken’s BTC/USD market during the same five-minute interval.
Blockstream CEO Adam Back suggested that a market maker on Kraken’s USD/CAD spot market may have exhausted its funds, causing prices to diverge from broader foreign exchange rates.
Back said arbitrage subsequently spread the pricing distortion to other Canadian-dollar trading pairs. Kraken has not confirmed Back’s proposed explanation.
Cointelegraph reached out to Kraken for comments but did not receive a response before publication.
Hong Kong pushes to bring crypto custodians, advisers under licensing rules
Hong Kong has published a bill that would bring crypto custodians, advisers and other virtual asset service providers under mandatory licensing or registration, extending oversight beyond trading platforms.
On Friday, the government officially published its Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026, proposing to regulate four activities, including virtual asset dealing, advisory, management and custody. Firms carrying out those activities would need to obtain a license from or register with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).
The proposed amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance would subject providers to fit-and-proper checks and other regulatory requirements. Banks and stored-value facility licensees supervised by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority would also have to register with the SFC to offer virtual asset services.
SFC chief executive Julia Leung said the proposal would strengthen investor protections and provide clearer paths for responsible innovation. The bill is set for its first reading in the Legislative Council on Dec. 2.
In October, Hong Kong said it would introduce legislation covering those four activities before the end of 2026, following consultations on the proposed framework.
The expanded regime has raised implementation concerns. In January, the Hong Kong Securities & Futures Professionals Association warned that introducing licenses without transitional arrangements could force existing businesses to suspend operations while their applications are reviewed. The association called for a six- to 12-month grace period.
Bitcoin falls below $60K for first time since July amid broader market selloff
Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since July, extending its recent losses amid a broader selloff in technology stocks and other risk assets.
Bitcoin (BTC) had fallen as low as $58,811 before recovering slightly to trade around $59,503, down 5.6% over the past 24 hours as of 16:52 UTC on Friday, according to CoinGecko data. The cryptocurrency has fallen 13.8% over the past week and nearly 30% over the past month.
The decline came amid a broader selloff in US equities. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.28% at 22,617.73, while the S&P 500 fell 3.69% to 6,910.77 on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance.
Shares of Anthropic (ANT), which made its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, closed down 8.50% at $88.91 amid concerns over valuations and spending in the artificial intelligence sector.

articles.title: Wagyu's $13.5 million token crash exposes another coin with 99.9% held by one wallet
articles.text:
Quick Take
- On November 20, 420 Hyperliquid accounts paid about $14 million for XMR1 sold by one wallet.
- The deployer that supplied the XMR1 seller held 99.97% of ZEC1 at 13:16 UTC on November 20.
- Wagyu’s bridge displayed an outage notice on November 21, leaving holders without a clear answer on redemptions.
Wagyu’s Monero-linked token plunged on Hyperliquid on Nov. 20 in a sell-off that generated about $14 million in gross proceeds for the seller, according to blockchain data firm Bitquery. The account that sent XMR1 to that wallet also created Wagyu’s Zcash-linked token, ZEC1, and held 99.97% of its supply at 13:16 UTC that day.
ZEC1 trades separately from XMR1. A transfer from the shared deployer could put a large block of ZEC1 in the hands of a seller, just as the XMR1 transfers did in the Monero-linked market. The Industry Spread reported that a Nov. 21 balance check put the same account’s holdings at about 20.99 million ZEC1. The figure counts wrapped tokens on Hyperliquid. How much native Zcash the bridge could pay out is a separate question.
Bitquery traced three transfers totaling about 5 million XMR1 from the deployer to the selling wallet between 04:46 and 05:16 UTC. The seller had moved only a fraction of that amount through the order book by Bitquery’s 13:00 UTC cutoff. The tally covered 369,623 XMR1 sold to 420 buying accounts. The token’s spot price fell from about $500 to about $1 in roughly half an hour. The first large sales began at 04:49 UTC, and Bitquery tracked smaller sales as late as 10:28 UTC.
Three-quarters of the proceeds came from buy orders already on Hyperliquid’s order book. The largest buying account paid about $4 million. The buyers’ final losses depend on what they can recover.
CryptoSlate previously reported on a separate trading-key risk on Hyperliquid following the Lighter incident.
Redeeming wrapped tokens depends on Wagyu’s bridge
Wagyu’s documentation describes how users deposit native Monero or Zcash to receive XMR1 or ZEC1 on Hyperliquid. To redeem, a holder sends the wrapped token through the bridge, which pays out the corresponding native coin.
Wagyu’s homepage and its bridge page displayed a temporary outage notice on Nov. 21. The bridge widget was still checking availability, leaving it unclear whether holders could complete redemptions.
Wagyu operator @PerpetualCow said on Nov. 20 that the XMR1 deployer key had been stored on an old server at a hosting provider that was breached. He said he would personally reimburse people who lost money and relaunch Wagyu, without giving a timetable.
Bitquery found no incoming transfers from other Hyperliquid accounts to the ten largest buying accounts between 06:00 and 13:16 UTC on Nov. 20. That check ended less than half an hour after the operator’s 12:48 UTC post. Completed reimbursements remained unverified.

articles.title: Google's Quantum Chip Beats Classical Limits in 'Impossible' Game - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Willow won the four-qubit magic square game 98.3% of the time, versus an 88.9% classical ceiling.
- Separate tests involved 71 qubits in a coordination game and 105 in a shallow-circuit task.
- The 105-qubit benchmark uses a conjectured classical bound and does not establish fault-tolerant computing.
Google says its Willow quantum processor won a mathematical coordination game 98.3% of the time, above the 88.9% maximum attainable by classical strategies, in a Science study published Thursday.
The experiment tests quantum contextuality, so measurement outcomes depend on what else is measured alongside them. Google researchers explained that “you cannot assign fixed, pre-existing values to everything you might measure.”
Don’t panic. The result does not mean Google has a commercial quantum computer, nor that its largest experiment beat every classical machine. The 98.3% figure came from four qubits—the basic unit of information used to encode data in quantum computing—the 105-qubit run tested a different, more limited challenge.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Google with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
The first test used the Mermin-Peres magic square game, which asks two players to fill intersecting parts of a three-by-three grid without communicating. Their answers must obey conflicting row-and-column rules and match at the shared square.
A prearranged classical strategy can succeed on no more than eight of nine assignments, or 88.9%. Entangled qubits can theoretically win every round, while Google’s physical processor won 98.3% across 900,000 trials, according to the researchers.
The researchers wrote that “our qubits coordinated better than any pre-written table allows.” Unavoidable hardware noise prevented the result from reaching the quantum ideal.
Google also measured contextuality. Any model with predetermined outcomes scores at most 4; quantum theory allows 6. Willow registered 5.590, with a reported uncertainty of 0.008.
Scaling up, with caveats
A separate GHZ parity game asked up to 71 entangled qubits to deliver coordinated binary answers. Success was measured against the strongest classical winning rate, which approaches 50% with more players; Google remained above that limit throughout its tests, despite accumulating hardware noise.
Researchers also verified genuine entanglement across 45 qubits. In the hidden linear function task, a shallow quantum circuit had to produce a binary string satisfying mathematical constraints. The processor reached roughly 60% success using 105 qubits.
Google says the tasks exposed small, systematic errors that conventional randomized tests can hide. Its corporate blog called contextuality testing “a sensitive new method to catch subtle hardware errors,” potentially helping engineers evaluate circuits used for chemistry and materials research.
The work follows Google's October report of a 40-fold error reduction in preparing magic states, a resource needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
For Bitcoin, the looming danger is that a future fault-tolerant quantum computer could break digital signatures, but that is still far from happening. Google’s 105-qubit task was instead a shallow mathematical circuit, and its largest instance still failed in about four out of 10 runs.

articles.title: UK to ban crypto exchanges from making markets on their own platforms as Bitcoin rules change
articles.text:
Quick Take
- From October 2027, firms making markets on qualifying crypto platforms can do so without principal-dealing permission for that activity.
- A UK venue operator is barred from making markets on its own platform and needs separate permission for matched-principal client execution.
- Eligible existing UK crypto firms seeking transitional protection must apply by February 28, 2027, for the permissions their activities require.
The UK is carving out a role for third-party firms that make markets in spot Bitcoin. From Oct. 25, 2027, they can buy and sell on qualifying crypto trading platforms without permission to deal as principal for that activity. The Financial Conduct Authority’s final rules bar UK platform operators from making markets on their own venues.
HM Treasury made the amending regulations on Nov. 18, 2026, adding Article 9UA to the UK’s regulated activities framework. The provision excludes market making on a qualifying cryptoasset trading platform from Article 9T, which covers dealing in qualifying cryptoassets as principal. A separate part of Article 9UA excludes trading strictly for a firm’s own purposes when it provides no service to anyone else.
A qualifying platform brings together multiple third-party buyers and sellers so their orders can result in trades in qualifying cryptoassets. The exclusion covers market making in those assets, including spot Bitcoin.
In its draft guidance, the FCA describes a market maker as a firm that stands ready to buy and sell listed assets on a continuing basis at prices it sets. The regulator proposes that responding to requests for quotes on the platform can also qualify.
Where firms still need permission
CryptoSlate previously covered how the FCA’s final crypto rules govern venue access and authorization when the new regime begins.
Operating a UK qualifying cryptoasset trading platform requires FCA authorization. The FCA’s final venue rules require operators to identify, document and monitor market-making users and disclose the terms of relevant incentives. A separate affiliate may trade on the venue under the same access rules as other users.
An operator can step between buyer and seller to execute client orders on its own platform as a matched principal when it holds the appropriate additional permission and follows venue rules that give it no discretion over how orders are matched. An operator that executes client orders against its own capital away from its own venue needs principal-dealing permission and must disclose its role and manage conflicts.
Firms that take orders from customers have to assess their permissions separately. Dealing as an agent or arranging deals can require permission. Firms executing or forwarding orders covered by the FCA’s rules for UK retail and elective professional clients must use a UK qualifying cryptoasset execution venue.
The FCA’s application window closes Feb. 28, 2027, for eligible firms with an existing UK cryptoasset business that want transitional protection for regulated activities. Market making that falls within Article 9UA carries no principal-dealing application requirement for that activity.
The FCA’s consultation on the carve-out closed Nov. 18, 2026. Its consultation page targets January 2027 for final guidance, while the consultation paper gives spring 2027.

articles.title: Upbit, Bithumb Halt CYBER Transfers After Suspected Bridge Exploit
articles.text:
South Korean exchanges halt CYBER transfers amid suspected bridge exploit
Cyber reported unexpected minting of CYBER tokens on Solana, followed by tokens moving out of its Ethereum bridge lockbox, prompting an investigation.
South Korean crypto exchanges Upbit and Bithumb suspended deposits and withdrawals of CYBER after the project reported suspicious activity involving its cross-chain bridge.
On Sunday, Bithumb announced it would suspend deposits and withdrawals because of suspected security issues. The exchange said trading will continue, while transfers would resume once network stability was assured. Upbit also announced a temporary suspension of CYBER deposits and withdrawals.
On Saturday, Cyber said it detected unexpected minting of CYBER tokens on Solana, followed by a transfer of tokens out of its bridge’s Ethereum lockbox.
Cyber, formerly CyberConnect, operates an Ethereum layer-2 network designed for social applications.
The project said it was investigating the incident and assessing which assets and bridge routes were affected. It advised users to avoid using the bridge or depositing CYBER to exchanges while the investigation continues.
The suspensions come days after South Korea’s Financial Services Commission announced plans to allow exchanges to halt deposits and withdrawals when hacking is suspected, rather than waiting for a confirmed breach.
Earlier in November, South Korean exchange GOPAX also suspended trading, deposits and standard withdrawals after receiving a hacking threat, despite saying no breach had occurred.
Related: Chainflip confirms $12M hack, offers attacker 10% bounty

articles.title: XRP's institutional adoption story has a catch that investors may be overlooking
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The XRP Ledger Foundation assessed all ten GL1 principles, and CertiK independently verified selected architecture and resiliency controls.
- Aviva’s tokenized sterling class deals through its administrator, with XRP Ledger transaction fees paid by the manager or platform.
- Eligible Ondo investors can deal in RLUSD, while the account responsible for ledger fees or reserves still needs XRP.
A technical review of selected XRP Ledger controls gives financial institutions more evidence as they consider bringing tokenized funds onto the network. Two existing products show where XRP comes in. Investors in Aviva’s tokenized sterling share class can subscribe and redeem without buying XRP. Eligible Ondo investors can deal in the dollar stablecoin RLUSD. The accounts responsible for network fees or reserves still need XRP.
The XRP Ledger Foundation said on Nov. 18 it had assessed the network against all ten principles of the Global Layer One Market Infrastructure Toolkit. It dated an independent report from blockchain security firm CertiK Nov. 13. On Nov. 19, CertiK said it independently checked selected technical controls under Architecture and Resiliency, using evidence that included code, configurations, logs and test results.
Legal basis and settlement finality were part of the Foundation’s own assessment. The GL1 toolkit gives institutions a common set of questions for their own due diligence. The Foundation says the exercise confers no regulatory approval or certification. Both fund designs were in place before the November disclosures.
How Aviva and Ondo handle fund dealing
Aviva put £50 million into the tokenized sterling share class it announced on Oct. 26. The approximately £22 billion quoted at launch was the size of the underlying Sterling Liquidity Fund. The smaller figure measures Aviva’s own investment in the class.
Under the fund prospectus, an investor sends a subscription through the administrator, which deals in cash off-chain and records the shares on its register. The platform issues the matching tokens after the subscription money arrives and the shares are issued. On redemption, the administrator processes the order and updates the register before the tokens are burned. The manager reconciles the two records daily. If the share register and the ledger diverge, the prospectus gives the register the final say over legal ownership.
Digital custodian Komainu holds the tokens in wallets for eligible investors. Ordinary investor-to-investor transfers are unavailable under the model. Aviva’s prospectus assigns the ledger transaction fees to the manager or tokenization platform, so investors can use the share class without buying XRP themselves. The fee provision leaves account reserve funding unspecified.
Ondo’s ledger handles more of the transaction. In June 2025 Ondo launched its tokenized U.S. Treasury fund OUSG on the XRP Ledger. Eligible investors can subscribe and redeem around the clock in RLUSD. The OUSG product terms require onboarding and eligibility as both an accredited investor and a qualified purchaser. An investor using its own ledger account can deal in RLUSD while still needing XRP for the fees and reserves that account is responsible for.
Ondo’s May 2026 bank-payout pilot used a different route. Ripple redeemed some OUSG on the ledger, then Mastercard routed the payout instruction and J.P. Morgan’s Kinexys sent U.S. dollars to Ripple’s bank account in Singapore. Ondo’s disclosures give no figures for routine on-ledger dealing and leave the reserve funder unspecified.
What it takes to run an XRP Ledger account
The network destroys XRP used for transaction fees. The documented minimum for a standard transaction is 0.00001 XRP, and it can rise under load. Account reserves work differently. The mainnet base reserve is 1 XRP, and an account typically needs another 0.2 XRP for each eligible ledger object it owns, subject to exceptions. Reserve XRP stays in the balance and can still cover fees. The account responsible for a fee or reserve needs to have the XRP for it.
Evidence of a bigger XRP requirement would come from fund terms that call for XRP settlement or collateral, or from repeated XRP transfers or posted collateral linked to identified fund accounts. Matching those transactions to product terms or settlement records would show what the XRP is doing. A wallet balance could simply keep the account funded for future fees and reserves.

articles.title: Chainflip Confirms $12M Hack, Offers Hacker 10% Bounty
articles.text:
Chainflip confirms $12M hack, offers attacker 10% bounty
Chainflip offered the attacker a 10% bounty to return 90% of the stolen funds by Nov. 23, promising to treat the return as a white-hat recovery and withdraw law enforcement complaints.
Cross-chain swap protocol Chainflip confirmed that an attacker stole about $12 million in Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins from its vaults on Saturday, expanding the initially reported $4.86 million loss.
In a statement addressed to the attacker, Chainflip Labs said 122.86 Bitcoin (BTC), 520.22 Ether (ETH), 3.25 million USDC and 758,141 USDT were stolen in the Saturday incident.
The company offered the attacker a 10% bounty to return the remaining 90% of stolen assets by 18:38 UTC on Nov. 23. Chainflip said it would treat the return as a white-hat recovery and withdraw its reports and complaints to law enforcement if the funds were returned before the deadline.
According to CoinGecko data, Chainflip’s FLIP token plunged 42.9% over the past 24 hours.
Chainflip said it had traced preparations for the attack to Tornado Cash funding on Nov. 11 and a validator account registered on Friday.
The company said it had identified the mechanism behind the cryptographic key exposure and taken steps to prevent similar attacks. It also said it obtained identifying information linked to the attacker that could assist law enforcement.
“We hold identifying information on the validator and servers used, your addresses are flagged across every major analytics firm, and every Tornado Cash withdrawal is being watched,” Chainflip said.
Related: Binance hacker moves nearly $600M in ETH, routes funds through THORChain, Chainflip

articles.title: Fucoidan Umi No Shizuku khẳng định dấu ấn thương hiệu tại Top 10 Thương hiệu Xuất sắc Châu Á Thái Bình Dương 2026
articles.text:
Khẳng định định hướng phát triển thương hiệu
Công ty TNHH Umi No Shizuku, đơn vị nhập khẩu và phân phối sản phẩm Thực phẩm Bảo vệ Sức khỏe Fucoidan Umi No Shizuku tại Việt Nam, được vinh danh trong Top 10 Thương hiệu Xuất sắc Châu Á Thái Bình Dương 2026. Danh hiệu đánh dấu một cột mốc trong hành trình phát triển thương hiệu, đồng thời tạo động lực để doanh nghiệp tiếp tục hoàn thiện chất lượng sản phẩm và dịch vụ.
Trong bối cảnh người tiêu dùng ngày càng quan tâm đến việc chăm sóc sức khỏe chủ động, các yếu tố như nguồn gốc xuất xứ, thành phần và tính minh bạch của thông tin sản phẩm trở thành cơ sở quan trọng khi lựa chọn. Nắm bắt xu hướng này, Umi No Shizuku định hướng phát triển thương hiệu dựa trên chất lượng, uy tín và trách nhiệm với khách hàng.
Fucoidan Umi No Shizuku - Sản phẩm chính hãng từ Nhật Bản
Fucoidan Umi No Shizuku là sản phẩm có nguồn gốc từ Nhật Bản, được nghiên cứu, sản xuất và đóng gói tại Nhật Bản, sau đó nhập khẩu và phân phối tại thị trường Việt Nam, và các nước khác trên thế giới. Sản phẩm được kết hợp các thành phần từ tảo nâu Mozuku, tảo nâu Mekabu và nấm Agaricus, hướng đến nhóm người tiêu dùng quan tâm đến bổ sung dinh dưỡng và chăm sóc sức khỏe chủ động.
Chất Fucoidan được quan tâm trong nghiên cứu y học về các lợi ích trong việc chăm sóc sức khỏe hằng ngày. Nó có nguồn gốc từ các loại tảo nâu. Tuy nhiên, chất Fucoidan được chiết xuất từ nhiều loại tảo nâu khác nhau, sẽ có hoạt tính và công dụng khác nhau. Dựa trên các bài nghiên cứu y học, chất Fucoidan chiết xuất từ tảo nâu Mozuku có hoạt tính hỗ trợ việc tế bào chết theo chương trình (chương trình apoptosis), chất Fucoidan chiết xuất từ tảo nâu Mekabu có hoạt tính hỗ trợ ngăn chặn mạch máu mới ở xung quanh tế bào bất thường.
Song song với việc đưa sản phẩm đến gần hơn với người tiêu dùng Việt Nam, Công ty TNHH Umi No Shizuku chú trọng cung cấp thông tin rõ ràng về thành phần, nguồn gốc và cách sử dụng. Doanh nghiệp cũng hướng đến nâng cao chất lượng tư vấn, giúp khách hàng có thêm cơ sở để lựa chọn sản phẩm phù hợp với nhu cầu cá nhân.
Lấy niềm tin khách hàng làm nền tảng
Trong thị trường sản phẩm chăm sóc sức khỏe ngày càng đa dạng, thương hiệu có uy tín không chỉ đến từ nguồn gốc sản phẩm mà còn được xây dựng qua chất lượng dịch vụ và sự nhất quán trong hoạt động phân phối. Vì vậy, Umi No Shizuku tập trung hoàn thiện quy trình vận hành, nâng cao chất lượng chăm sóc khách hàng và tăng cường tính minh bạch trong việc cung cấp thông tin.
Đại diện Công ty TNHH Umi No Shizuku chia sẻ: “UMI NO SHIZUKU – Thương hiệu Fucoidan đến từ Nhật Bản, mang trong mình sứ mệnh chăm sóc sức khỏe và nâng cao chất lượng cuộc sống cho cộng đồng. Với các sản phẩm được sản xuất tại Nhật Bản, UMI NO SHIZUKU luôn chú trọng chất lượng, sự an toàn và uy tín trong từng sản phẩm đến tay người tiêu dùng.
Bằng sự tận tâm và nỗ lực không ngừng, thương hiệu từng bước khẳng định vị thế và xây dựng niềm tin với khách hàng tại thị trường Việt Nam.
Hướng đến phát triển bền vững
Trong thời gian tới, doanh nghiệp cho biết sẽ tiếp tục chú trọng chất lượng trong hoạt động nhập khẩu và phân phối, nâng cao trải nghiệm tư vấn, hoàn thiện dịch vụ chăm sóc khách hàng và cung cấp thông tin sản phẩm minh bạch.
Danh hiệu Top 10 Thương hiệu Xuất sắc Châu Á Thái Bình Dương 2026 không chỉ là dấu mốc đáng nhớ mà còn đặt ra yêu cầu tiếp tục duy trì những giá trị đã xây dựng. Với định hướng phát triển lâu dài, Umi No Shizuku kỳ vọng củng cố niềm tin của người tiêu dùng, nâng cao chất lượng dịch vụ và đồng hành cùng khách hàng trên hành trình chăm sóc sức khỏe chủ động.
Thực phẩm bảo vệ sức khỏe Fucoidan Umi No Shizuku chứa Fucoidan chiết xuất từ tảo nâu Mozuku và Mekabu, có nguồn gốc từ Nhật Bản. Sản phẩm được nghiên cứu, sản xuất, đóng gói tại Nhật Bản, hướng đến nhu cầu hỗ trợ nâng cao sức đề kháng và hỗ trợ giảm tác hại do hóa trị, xạ trị. Tại Việt Nam, sản phẩm được Công ty TNHH Umi No Shizuku nhập khẩu, phân phối chính hãng với dạng bột, viên nang và nước.
