Thời gian cập nhật: 06:00-22/11/2026
Giá vàng thế giới hôm nay 22/11
Giá vàng thế giới mở cửa đầu tuần ở mức 3.869 USD/ounce. Kim loại quý có thời điểm tăng lên 3.901 USD/ounce nhưng nhanh chóng đảo chiều. Lo ngại lạm phát kéo dài và căng thẳng tại Trung Đông không đủ hỗ trợ giá vàng.
Áp lực bán gia tăng sau khi doanh số bán lẻ tháng 10 của Mỹ chỉ tăng 0,2%. Giá vàng sau đó xuyên thủng mốc 3.800 USD/ounce. Biên bản cuộc họp tháng 10 của Fed cho thấy các nhà hoạch định chính sách chưa thống nhất về định hướng lãi suất. Một số quan chức cân nhắc tăng lãi suất 0,5 điểm phần trăm trong tháng 12.
Đến ngày thứ Năm, giá vàng tiếp tục giảm dù số đơn xin trợ cấp thất nghiệp lần đầu tại Mỹ tăng lên 203.000. Chỉ số sản xuất của Fed chi nhánh Philadelphia giảm mạnh xuống 6,3 điểm. Áp lực giá đầu vào vẫn cao, làm gia tăng lo ngại về lạm phát.
Đà bán tháo tăng tốc trong phiên cuối tuần khi thị trường chứng khoán, đặc biệt là nhóm cổ phiếu công nghệ, chịu áp lực. Một số nhà đầu tư bán vàng để bù đắp thua lỗ và đáp ứng nhu cầu thanh khoản ở các thị trường khác.
Giá vàng giao ngay có thời điểm xuống 3.502,93 USD/ounce, mức thấp nhất trong tuần. Sau đó, kim loại quý phục hồi nhưng vẫn kết thúc tuần quanh 3.539 USD/ounce, giảm gần 9% so với cuối tuần trước. Giá vàng kỳ hạn tháng 12/2026 giao dịch quanh 3.537 USD/ounce.
Sean Lusk, đồng giám đốc bộ phận phòng ngừa rủi ro thương mại tại Walsh Trading, nhận định giá vàng có thể giảm thêm 300 USD/ounce nếu không giữ được vùng hỗ trợ 3.500 USD/ounce. Trên thị trường hợp đồng tương lai, ngưỡng tương ứng là 3.573 USD/ounce.
Theo ông Lusk, giá vàng đã giảm 5% chỉ trong vài ngày. Với mức 3.573 USD/ounce của hợp đồng vàng giao tháng 12, kim loại quý đã giảm khoảng 20% so với mức đóng cửa cuối năm ngoái là 4.341 USD/ounce.
Nếu mốc 3.500 USD/ounce bị xuyên thủng, vùng hỗ trợ tiếp theo có thể nằm trong khoảng 3.256-3.280 USD/ounce. Đây là vùng đáy được hình thành vào tháng 7/2025.
Chuyên gia này cho rằng đà giảm của vàng xuất phát từ nhiều nguyên nhân. Nhà đầu tư đã nắm giữ vị thế mua quá lớn trên thị trường kim loại quý, trong khi nguy cơ Fed tiếp tục tăng lãi suất gây bất lợi cho vàng. Bên cạnh đó, đà bán tháo cổ phiếu buộc một số nhà đầu tư phải bán vàng để bù đắp thua lỗ và giảm rủi ro.
Yếu tố mùa vụ cũng gây thêm áp lực. Tháng 11 thường là giai đoạn kém tích cực đối với giá vàng.
Về triển vọng, Lusk khuyến nghị nhà đầu tư chưa nên vội mua vàng. Ông cho rằng thời điểm phù hợp hơn có thể là đầu tháng 12, ngay trước cuộc họp chính sách của Fed.
Trong nước, giá vàng miếng SJC sáng 21/11 được niêm yết ở mức 128,5 triệu đồng/lượng mua vào và 133,5 triệu đồng/lượng bán ra.
So với cuối tuần trước, khi giá vàng SJC ở mức 134,5-137,5 triệu đồng/lượng, giá mua vào đã giảm 6 triệu đồng/lượng, còn giá bán ra giảm 4 triệu đồng/lượng. Khoảng cách giữa giá mua vào và bán ra ở mức 5 triệu đồng/lượng.

articles.title: 4 random apps you might not realize work with Android Auto - Engadget
articles.text:
4 random apps you might not realize work with Android Auto
Some of these apps will be familiar, while others you may not have heard of.
Android Auto users typically utilize just a few basic apps like Google Maps for directions and Spotify for music. They don't dive into the developer menu; they don't make any serious changes to the way Android Auto works; and they don't know they could be spending all those minutes waiting for someone in a parking lot playing games directly on the car's infotainment display. But the platform's compatible app library runs much deeper, well beyond navigation and streaming.
Android Auto actually supports a surprising range of communication and meeting tools, like WhatsApp and Google Meet, and even a bunch of other apps to help you navigate more efficiently. Each one adds layer after layer of functionality that most users never think to explore. Discovering new apps can genuinely change how you commute while also making it possible to enjoy your drive just a tiny bit more.
Take your work on the road with Google Meet
Android Auto comes with some extra functionality for those in the corporate world, as several popular apps come with Android Auto support for meetings and calls, with Google Meet leading the way. Because Meet is Google's own app, it fits naturally into the Android Auto experience. You can see your upcoming meetings on the car display and join a call with a single tap, all in audio-only mode so your eyes stay on the road. Whether it's a short check-in with your manager or a longer team call, Meet makes it easy to keep up with your schedule even if you have to drive around.
Google's app isn't the only option, though. Zoom, Webex by Cisco and Microsoft Teams all work on Android Auto, offering users the opportunity to join video conferences with audio only. Some apps take integration a step further. Microsoft Teams, for instance, lets users check their calendar and place calls directly from the car display. Google Meet also displays upcoming meetings on your schedule. These features are particularly useful if you're often traveling from location to location but still have to participate in meetings along the way. They also help if you have to leave early to pick up the kids from school while a meeting is still on your calendar.
One thing to mention about these apps is that, depending on your employer, restrictions may apply. Certain companies require corporate apps like Google Meet and Microsoft Teams to run inside an isolated Android Work Profile. In such situations, Android Auto may block calendar sync or prevent the app from appearing on the screen. There's a Work Mode in the works on Android Auto, though, so it may soon be easier to reach all those apps that are locked out by your employer.
Stay fueled up with Fuelio
With gas prices being what they are these days, it's more important than ever to know where to fuel up. Apps like Fuelio can help with that when you're looking for a place to put gas in your car without breaking the bank. Fuelio tracks fill-ups, odometer readings and fuel prices, then calculates your average fuel economy and cost per mile over time. You can even use various filters to display gas stations that were updated within the past day, or those that are most appreciated by users.
Google Maps and other similar tools can surface the nearest gas stations and even tell you the latest prices, but Fuelio gives more in-depth information regarding fuel type, distance and more. Plus, when you throw in all the other features, it's a much better fit if you want to know exactly how much your car is costing you. While Fuelio is free to use with Android Auto, there is a premium version available that costs money.
Stay charged up with PlugShare
If you're driving an EV, then the app you absolutely must use through Android Auto is PlugShare. This free tool (the paid version removes ads) gives you access to a crowd-sourced map that lets you see the nearest charging stations along your route. Its real strength is the community behind it, because drivers leave real-time feedback, uploading photos of the charger layout, reporting broken plugs and checking in after charging. That gives you a clear picture of what to expect before you pull in, so a station that looks fine on paper but has been out of service for days won't catch you off guard.
There are loads of filters you can play with, letting you choose the exact plug type, charging speed and network. You can also check which amenities are nearby, such as restrooms or a place to grab coffee while you wait. It's also a great tool for long-distance drives, as it automatically recommends charging stops along the way based on your specific EV model's range. That goes a long way toward easing the range anxiety that comes with getting an electric car. The one downside is that the data is only as good as its contributors, so stations in less-traveled areas may have fewer recent reports.
Go offline without losing your way with HERE WeGo
Data can be expensive, especially if you use your phone a ton. When you're traveling abroad, costs go up by quite a bit, so you should make the most of your home Wi-Fi. Apps like HERE WeGo through Android Auto offer offline navigation, so your data plan isn't ever a concern. HERE WeGo lets you download maps for entire countries so you always know where you're going. For some countries, you can download maps for certain areas, such as for Germany where you can grab a map for Berlin and another for Hamburg. In the United States, you can grab maps for entire states, but not separate cities.
There are plenty of features to fiddle with to make this app yours, like choosing which fuel type your car uses, having the metric vs. imperial system displayed the way you prefer and so on. The app will flag parking spots and rest areas along the route, and you can even tell it what types of things to avoid. For instance, Waze lets you avoid ferries and highways, but HERE WeGo can have you avoid tunnels and U-turns too. The app can take things one step further and even use visual references on route, which means it will tell you to make a right at the traffic light or when you reach a certain landmark.
Bonus: Get more out of messaging
Yes, Android Auto will read out your texts — we all know that. But it can also handle other apps, reading out your messages if you so desire and then letting you use your voice to reply. WhatsApp is the clearest example of this working well, as Android Auto can read your messages aloud. Then, Gemini asks if you want to reply and will type out the words for you. Signal offers similar read-aloud and reply functionality; so do Facebook Messenger, Microsoft Teams and Google Chat, to name a few.
This feature can be super useful when you're driving as you can stay connected without taking your eyes off the road. The ability to reply to messages will also help you stay on top of any emergencies without having to pull over. However, as with any AI typing tool, you should expect some mistakes here and there.
Adding all these apps is straightforward as you only have to install them from the Google Play Store on your phone. Compatible apps will automatically pop up on your Android Auto launcher. You can go into the Android Auto settings and reorganize the apps if you want to make some more easily accessible. Android Auto's compatibility list is wider than most people assume, but the best setup prioritizes the tools that you actually use when you're behind the wheel.

articles.title: How Tamagotchis got us hooked on digital pets
articles.text:
If you were are a kid in the late 1990s, there’s a near-100 percent chance you either had a Tamagotchi or knew someone who did. The tiny digital pets came out of nowhere and became an overnight sensation, as millions of kids signed up to parent a crying, hungry, constantly dirty creature. Until they went to school, anyway, at which point their parents were given some new responsibilities they neither asked for nor wanted.
How Tamagotchis got us hooked on digital pets
On Version History: Why millions of people signed up to feed, change, and play with a beeping little keychain.
On this episode of Version History, we dig deep into the story of the Tamagotchi. That story has its 30th anniversary this week, even though the real craze only lasted a few years. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Mia Sato and Victoria Song to discuss the origins of the Tamagotchi, the product’s many iterations, its incredible engagement tactics, and whether any of us could tolerate the Tama experience three decades later. (We… could not.)
This is the second episode of the sixth season of Version History, all about tech for your pets — and tech that is pets. Last week we fell back in love with the Sony Aibo, and there’s lots more to come this season. f you want to be sure not to miss anything, there are a few ways to subscribe:
If you’re a Verge subscriber, you can also get access to Version History (and all our other podcasts) with no ads. All you have to do is visit your account settings.

articles.title: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die
articles.text:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.
They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.
Fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.
Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine said.
The experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”
When he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined quickly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.
When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.
Convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.
They considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.
Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.
By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.
For six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.
When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.
During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.
He devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.
It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.
According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.
For Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.
The idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.
“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran said.
Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, said Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.
“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he said of the new work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.
Another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, said Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.
Ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he said. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.
However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet said. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.
For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.
“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet said, “right there under our feet.”

articles.title: 4 iPad Pro alternatives for those looking to ditch Apple - Engadget
articles.text:
4 iPad Pro alternatives for those looking to ditch Apple
Apple's iPad Pro is far from the only game in town.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
If you're looking for the best tablet on the market — or at least the best with a mobile operating system — it is undoubtedly the 2025 iPad Pro. The latest iPad Pro sports Apple's M5 chip, which powered the previous year's MacBook Pro. It's a chip so powerful that most users are unlikely to brush against its performance ceiling. The tandem OLED display is similarly overkill, and is a feature no other tablet available in North America has. Apple is so far ahead of its competitors in the high-end tablet market that it feels like Tim Cook wanted to taunt them with its existence.
But the iPad Pro is not perfect. The locked-down iPadOS experience means you're limited to the apps Apple approves of. It also means you cannot install apps without signing into an Apple account. If you don't own other Apple devices, things can get awkward as the iPad becomes siloed away from the rest of your gadgets, requiring you to find workarounds for syncing files or notifications.
Thankfully, things are getting more interesting for tablets outside of Apple's walled garden. While no Android tablets can rival the iPad Pro's performance, many offer other advantages such as ecosystem synergy with Windows PCs, gaming features, expandable storage or more included accessories. And if performance is what you're after, it's worth a gander at Windows tablets now that Windows on ARM is coming into its own.
The direct competitor: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra
The easiest alternative to recommend is Samsung's newest flagship tablet, the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. The first thing you'll notice is its size: it looks like someone tore the screen off a full-sized laptop, with a 14.6-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2x display that dwarfs even the larger 13-inch iPad Pro. If you love watching videos on your tablet, this is the only device that can give the iPad's luxurious tandem OLED display a run for its money. It also has Samsung's anti-reflective coating, which the iPad lacks.
What you won't get with the Galaxy tablet, or with any Android tablet, is the iPad Pro's raw horsepower. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra's MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor is decently powerful, but it's nowhere near the desktop-class Apple M5 chip in the latest iPad Pro. That said, the Galaxy has more than enough firepower for games, video editing, and other taxing tasks, and it comes with 12GB of RAM (or 16GB on the 1TB storage version) to help get the job done.
Samsung's One UI is widely considered the best Android skin and an excellent alternative to iOS or iPadOS. It also has several features you won't find elsewhere in the Android space. If you have a Windows PC, One UI lets you use the tablet as a second PC display, for example, or share your mouse and keyboard with your computer.
Despite its reduced performance, the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra also competes with the iPad Pro on price. It starts at $1,400 for the 256GB model with 12GB of RAM and only gets steeper from there, maxing out at $2,000 for the 1TB model with 16GB of RAM.
The entertainment-focused alternative: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro
Until recently, Amazon made cheap, underpowered Fire tablets meant mostly for basic entertainment. The new Alexa Tablet 12 Pro bucks that trend. Alexa Tablets don't compare that favorably to the iPad Pro, but they're cheaper and make reasonable compromises. Amazon has also ditched its Fire OS Android skin in favor of a more traditional Android experience — crucially, with access to the Google Play Store.
Amazon's head of hardware, Panos Panay, told Engadget the screen was the one component of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro the company refused to compromise on. It has a slightly higher pixel density than the iPad Pro, with an optional matte coating similar to certain Samsung devices and Apple's iPhone Duo. Our review of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro found the MediaTek Dimensity 8400 chip inside presented no obstacles to productivity and entertainment tasks, but did stutter a bit while multitasking. You get eight and 16GB of RAM on the 128- and 256GB storage models, respectively.
If price is what turns you off from the iPad, Amazon's starting price of $500 will be very appealing. However, that's for just 128GB of storage, which will fill up quickly since it lacks a microSD card expansion slot. The Nanomatte display is an extra $50. If you want the top-spec 256GB model, expect to pay $680, with the Nanomatte display included.
The alternative for gamers: RedMagic Astra 2
If you want a powerful tablet with gaming-focused features at a more affordable price than the iPad Pro, look no further than the RedMagic Astra 2. Part of that lower price, though, is because the Astra 2 has a 9-inch screen, 2 inches smaller than the smallest iPad Pro. It makes sense for gaming — a large tablet can be tiring to hold up — but if you want a large screen for videos or productivity, this may not be the device for you.
The Astra 2 runs the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, making it arguably the most powerful Android tablet on this list, but still far short of Apple's M5 chip. The biggest barrier to consistent performance on mobile chips is cooling: Most Android devices with top-end chips throttle them to prevent overheating, but RedMagic compensates with a large vapor chamber and real liquid cooling to dissipate heat. GSMArena benchmarks show that the cooling gives the Astra 2 a slight advantage over the OnePlus Pad 4, which uses the same Snapdragon chip.
RedMagic has equipped the Astra 2 with a few bells and whistles Apple doesn't match. The display, though smaller, is more pixel-dense at 313 ppi vs. the iPad Pro's 264, while its 185Hz refresh rate also beats the iPad Pro's 120 (the newly updated iPad Mini is still stuck at 60Hz). It's a bit brighter, too. All of this enables a better gaming experience, which emphasizes who this tablet is for.
Price-to-performance is another bright spot for the Astra 2. RedMagic charges $750 for the base 256GB model with 12GB of RAM, or $850 for the 512GB configuration with 16GB of RAM. That makes it the best bang-for-the-buck option on this list, assuming you approve of its gaming-focused design.
The do-it-all alternative for Windows users: Microsoft Surface Pro
Android tablets have plenty of nifty features, but none equal the iPad Pro's desktop-class processing power. If that's what you want, look to Windows. The Microsoft Surface Pro is more complicated than any other tablet on this list, but that's because it has the full power of Windows 11 running on either a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus or X2 Elite processor.
The Snapdragon models are ARM-powered, just like the iPad. That gives them better battery life than traditional x86 Windows laptops, albeit at the cost of software support. Many apps aren't yet optimized for ARM, and you'll need to check whether the software you need is fully supported. Whether you want to deal with Windows 11 on a tablet is down to personal preference, but if you've used a Windows 11 PC in the past, the Surface Pro is no different. It's a marked departure from the touch-optimized interface of iPadOS or Android, but professionals in need of pro-grade software will be able to get more done on a Surface Pro than on an Android tablet, and arguably more than on an iPad Pro, depending on which software is required.
The Surface Pro is as expensive as it is capable. The X2 Plus-equipped 12-inch model starts at $1,140 for the 256GB model with 12GB of RAM and an LCD. The 13-inch Surface Pro starts at $1,200 for the same configuration. If you want an OLED screen that bumps the refresh rate from 90 Hz to 120, you'll also have to upgrade to the more powerful Snapdragon X2 Elite chip; that variant starts at $1,500, maxing out at $2,849 for the top configuration with 1TB of storage and 64GB of RAM.

articles.title: Your questions about Apple HomeView’s audio, answered
articles.text:
After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker. So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. Have more? I’ll answer them in the comments.
Your questions about Apple HomeView’s audio, answered
The smart display sounds good and works well as a touchscreen music controller, but CarPlay apps are messy.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
How does the HomeView sound compared to the HomePod Mini, Sonos One, and HomePod?
The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. Those are much better speakers. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling.
You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView:
The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.)
The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell.
Can you pair two HomeViews for stereo sound?
No. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms.
If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. The HomeView’s real benefit is the screen. I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! With a HomePod, you rely on Siri voice control or your Apple device to select content.
Can you AirPlay music/podcasts to the HomeView, and does audio handoff work?
You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. One addition with the HomeView: You can now hand off video.
In testing, handoff worked for Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Pocket Casts, YouTube Music, FaceTime, and phone calls — although phone calls sometimes dropped. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser.
One word of caution: Handoff is aggressive. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content.
Can you set a default speaker for the HomeView?
HomeView doesn’t let you set a default speaker or group to use instead of its built-in speaker. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly.
For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. If it’s been a while since you opened the app, it pops up the option to choose the last-used speakers.
Spotify has no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving — only I’m not driving; I’m in my kitchen!
Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker.
So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music.
Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Like second-class citizens.
Does Spotify work on the HomeView?
Spotify works on the HomeView, but with limitations that apply to all non-native and third-party apps: they only show up when your phone is connected to the HomeView via your profile, so only you can use them.
Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform. This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).
In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi. It also results in slower performance and a laggy, inconsistent experience compared to the native apps.
I tried several apps: Pocket Casts, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, Spotify, and Audible. They all appeared in my HomeView app drawer, and I could access them, choose content via streamlined interfaces, and then play audio on the HomeView or AirPlay from it to any speakers.
But CarPlay apps don’t work as well as the built-in audio apps — Music, Podcasts, and Safari. They take longer to load and respond more slowly. You also can’t type a search query in any of them, as you can in the native apps, because they don’t have a search field or keyboard. Instead, you have to scroll through content to find what you want or use Siri voice search.
Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”
There’s no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving; only I’m not driving — I’m in my kitchen! This shows how much of a CarPlay port the apps are; they haven’t been updated to account for the fact that this device is stationary and in your home. Case in point, when I first pulled up the Apple TV app (the only CarPlay video app currently supported), a warning popped up telling me to make sure I was stationary before watching any video.
Playing audio through CarPlay apps is also buggy. It didn’t always bring up the music control screen, so I had to use my iPhone to control it. Plus, the Audible app often refused to load at all and didn’t work with Siri voice search. Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”
CarPlay support feels like a stopgap, and Apple needs to work with developers to refine the software and add HomeView-specific controls for a better, more integrated experience.
Should you buy a HomeView as a smart speaker?
Much of the confusion around the HomeView stems from treating it like a smart speaker when it’s really a smart display. I get it; I’ve spent the last decade frustrated by smart displays from Google and Amazon that promise a lot but rarely do it all well.
If you don’t care about the other features of a smart display and just want a smart speaker, then the reason to buy a HomeView over a HomePod is if you have a use for it as a touchscreen music controller. This lets anyone in the household easily browse and control what’s playing. Bear in mind, though, Apple Music (with a subscription) is the only app anyone can use to play music on the HomeView, as CarPlay apps require a user profile.
If you want a smart speaker primarily to play music and are happy using your voice or phone to control it, go for a HomePod. If you use Spotify or other third-party music services, consider an Echo Dot or Google Home smart speaker; both let you set a default speaker and a default music provider — such as Spotify.
If you already own HomePods and use Apple Music, the HomeView’s touchscreen will fit in nicely as a simple way to control audio. Just don’t buy one expecting it to fully replace a dedicated smart speaker.

articles.title: How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
articles.text:
This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.
The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.
This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.
“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”
El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.
Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.
Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”
And the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched. The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.
As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees Celsius—breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees Celsius—and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.
Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested—though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.
All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.
While any year brings its own spates of bad weather—some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change—plenty of events this year have been attributed to El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.
In Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.
Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second-largest annual crop on record.
“Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” says FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market, and some people won’t be able to afford it.
An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño–prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.
One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.
The World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program says it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.
Cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, says Choularton, they can afford to reach fewer than a million.
Advanced warning is good, says Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.
Global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people, that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he says. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an important effect on people’s lives.”
Because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, says Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the big questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”

articles.title: Phát hiện cựu sinh viên tốt nghiệp cách đây 64 năm nay trở thành tỷ phú công nghệ, cam kết tặng trường cũ hơn 9.600 tỷ đồng: Lập kỷ lục lịch sử, tên ông được dùng để đặt tên cho trường kỹ thuật
articles.text:
Phát hiện cựu sinh viên tốt nghiệp cách đây 64 năm nay trở thành tỷ phú công nghệ, cam kết tặng trường cũ hơn 9.600 tỷ đồng: Lập kỷ lục lịch sử, tên ông được dùng để đặt tên cho trường kỹ thuật
Sau hơn sáu thập kỷ rời giảng đường, một cựu sinh viên đã đưa ngôi trường cũ đến dấu mốc chưa từng có.
Cựu sinh viên lập kỷ lục với khoản cam kết hơn 9.600 tỷ đồng
Ngày 22/1/2026, Đại học Cornell (Mỹ) công bố khoản cam kết tài trợ trị giá 371,5 triệu USD từ một cựu sinh viên tương đương khoảng 9.659 tỷ đồng theo tỷ giá quy đổi. Đây là khoản cam kết đơn lẻ lớn nhất trong lịch sử ngôi trường, đồng thời đánh dấu bước ngoặt quan trọng đối với hoạt động đào tạo và nghiên cứu kỹ thuật tại Cornell.
Người đứng sau khoản tài trợ khổng lồ này là David A. Duffield, doanh nhân công nghệ tốt nghiệp Cornell năm 1962 và nhận bằng MBA tại đây năm 1964. Tính đến thời điểm công bố khoản cam kết mới, đã 64 năm trôi qua kể từ khi ông hoàn thành chương trình đại học. Dù rời giảng đường từ lâu, Duffield vẫn duy trì mối quan hệ đặc biệt với nơi từng đào tạo mình.
Đáng chú ý, 371,5 triệu USD không phải khoản đóng góp đầu tiên của doanh nhân này. Tháng 3/2025, Cornell từng công bố khoản tài trợ 100 triệu USD của ông dành cho việc nâng cấp và mở rộng Duffield Hall, công trình phục vụ nghiên cứu và giảng dạy khoa học kỹ thuật. Tính cả những khoản hỗ trợ trước đây, tổng giá trị đóng góp của Duffield cho trường kỹ thuật đã vượt 520 triệu USD, tương đương hơn 13.500 tỷ đồng.
Trên phạm vi Đại học Cornell, tổng giá trị đóng góp tích lũy của ông đã đạt 550 triệu USD, tương đương khoảng 14.300 tỷ đồng. Con số này đưa Duffield vào nhóm những nhà tài trợ lớn nhất trong lịch sử của trường đại học.
Để ghi nhận sự đóng góp đặc biệt, Đại học Cornell quyết định đặt tên trường kỹ thuật trực thuộc là Cornell David A. Duffield College of Engineering. Ngôi trường có lịch sử gần 160 năm, đào tạo và nghiên cứu trong nhiều lĩnh vực công nghệ quan trọng. Việc mang tên một cựu sinh viên đánh dấu sự gắn bó lâu dài giữa nhà trường và doanh nhân từng trưởng thành từ chính những giảng đường này.
Trước khi trở thành nhà tài trợ kỷ lục, David Duffield đã xây dựng sự nghiệp đáng chú ý trong ngành phần mềm. Trong hơn 60 năm, ông sáng lập sáu doanh nghiệp phần mềm dành cho khách hàng tổ chức, nổi bật là PeopleSoft, Workday và Ridgeline. Ông thuộc nhóm rất hiếm nhà sáng lập tại Mỹ từng đưa hai doanh nghiệp do mình lãnh đạo lên sàn chứng khoán với mức định giá từ 1 tỷ USD trở lên. Theo Forbes, tài sản ròng năm 2026 của David Duffield ước tính khoảng 10,1 tỷ USD (ghi nhận khoảng 11,3 tỷ USD vào tháng 9/2026)
Dù đạt nhiều thành tựu kinh doanh, Duffield vẫn dành sự quan tâm cho giáo dục và nghiên cứu. Ông đánh giá cao khả năng sáng tạo, lãnh đạo và giải quyết vấn đề của những người tốt nghiệp từ Đại học Cornell mà mình từng làm việc cùng. Với doanh nhân này, hỗ trợ trường cũ là cách góp phần thúc đẩy những thế hệ kỹ sư và nhà nghiên cứu tiếp theo.
Hé lộ lý do vị doanh nhân giàu có không quên trường cũ
Đằng sau hành trình trở thành doanh nhân công nghệ của David Duffield là ảnh hưởng từ hai giảng viên tại Cornell: William L. Maxwell và Richard Conway. Họ là những người đã khơi dậy niềm yêu thích của ông đối với máy tính và lập trình từ thời công nghệ này còn ở giai đoạn đầu phát triển. Duffield từng nhắc đến cả hai như những người thầy có vai trò quan trọng trong sự nghiệp của mình.
Hai giảng viên đã phát triển một chương trình tạo báo cáo mang tên ASAP cho Cornell. Sau này, Duffield có cơ hội hợp tác với họ và nhà trường để triển khai chương trình tại hai doanh nghiệp đầu tiên do mình thành lập. Trải nghiệm ấy cho thấy những kiến thức và mối quan hệ hình thành trong thời sinh viên đã tiếp tục đồng hành với ông trên con đường kinh doanh.
Không chỉ các giảng viên, cha mẹ cũng ảnh hưởng sâu sắc đến quan niệm của Duffield về giáo dục. Mẹ ông là giáo viên tiểu học, còn cha làm quản lý dự án tại Bell Labs và từng giữ chức chủ tịch hội đồng giáo dục địa phương. Dù không có điều kiện hoàn thành chương trình đại học bốn năm, cả hai vẫn quyết tâm tạo cơ hội học tập tốt cho các con.
David Duffield và em trai Al Duffield đều theo học tại Đại học Cornell, lần lượt tốt nghiệp vào năm 1962 và 1965. Vị doanh nhân giàu có cũng từng chia sẻ rằng giáo dục là một phần trong những giá trị được gia đình ông coi trọng từ nhỏ. Vì vậy, việc đóng góp cho Đại học Cornell cũng mang ý nghĩa tiếp nối mong muốn mà cha mẹ đã dành cho hai anh em.
Khoản cam kết 371,5 triệu USD lần này không chỉ phục vụ một công trình riêng lẻ mà hướng đến việc tạo nguồn lực lâu dài cho trường kỹ thuật. Trong đó, 250 triệu USD sẽ dùng để thành lập Duffield Legacy Fund, quỹ hỗ trợ nhà trường theo đuổi các cơ hội phát triển chiến lược. Thêm 50 triệu USD dành cho những ưu tiên nhằm nâng cao chất lượng giáo dục.
Phần kinh phí còn lại sẽ hình thành Duffield Launch Fund, hỗ trợ các nhu cầu trước mắt như nâng cấp cơ sở vật chất, tăng cường điều kiện nghiên cứu và hỗ trợ giảng viên, sinh viên. Những lĩnh vực được chú trọng bao gồm công nghệ lượng tử, kỹ thuật phục vụ sức khỏe con người, trí tuệ nhân tạo và ra quyết định dựa trên dữ liệu. Đây là các hướng nghiên cứu cần nguồn lực đáng kể để phát triển bền vững.
Trước khoản cam kết kỷ lục, tên Duffield đã gắn với Duffield Hall, công trình được hoàn thành giai đoạn đầu năm 2004. Tòa nhà là nơi đặt các cơ sở nghiên cứu và giảng dạy về khoa học, kỹ thuật ở quy mô nano. Khoản tài trợ 100 triệu USD năm 2025 tiếp tục giúp mở rộng và nâng cấp công trình này.
Sau 64 năm kể từ ngày tốt nghiệp, David Duffield đã tạo nên một dấu ấn mới tại nơi mình từng theo học. Từ những bài học về máy tính thuở ban đầu đến ngôi trường kỹ thuật mang tên ông, hành trình ấy cho thấy sự gắn bó giữa một cựu sinh viên và trường cũ có thể kéo dài qua nhiều thế hệ. Khoản cam kết hơn 9.600 tỷ đồng không chỉ lập kỷ lục về giá trị mà còn được kỳ vọng tạo thêm cơ hội cho những sinh viên và nhà nghiên cứu trong tương lai.
Nguồn: Cornell University
